markdown:
Engineering hiring has become both easier and harder. There are plenty of applicants for most open roles, which makes it tempting to believe supply is not a problem, yet leaders still struggle to find people who can own a system, reason about trade-offs and work well with others. This guide covers how to measure engineering hiring, scope the main roles, assess skill, understand how AI tooling is changing the work and keep engineers.

It contains no market averages. Figures here are illustrative examples with stated assumptions. For real data use the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational profiles for software roles and any survey you have licensed, and check each source's definitions.

## How should engineering teams define hiring metrics?

Write them down: time-to-fill (approved requisition to accepted offer), offer acceptance (accepted over written offers), interview pass-through rate by stage, time-to-first-merged-change for new hires and early attrition. Time-to-first-merged-change is a practical, role-specific proxy for onboarding quality and is easier to measure than "productivity."

Compare across the same role family and level. A senior backend engineer, an engineering manager and a QA engineer have different markets and cycle times.

## Which roles need careful scoping?

| Role | Decide before writing the brief |
| :--- | :--- |
| Software engineer | Stack, scope of ownership, on-call duties, whether the work is product or platform |
| Platform or site reliability engineer | Infrastructure in use, incident load, how much is building versus operating |
| Data or machine learning engineer | Pipelines or models, production responsibility, tooling |
| Engineering manager | Number of reports, hands-on expectation, hiring responsibility, relationship with product |
| Quality or test engineer | Automation versus exploratory, release process, tools |
| Technical program manager | Cross-team scope, authority, reporting line |
| Product designer | Research support, design system maturity, collaboration with engineers |

Level matters more than title. Write what a person at that level is expected to own: a feature, a service, a domain or a team. A shared leveling guide, even a short one, reduces mismatched offers and unfair comparisons.

## How should you assess engineers?

Use work that reflects the job and keep it short.

1. **Code review exercise.** Give a realistic change with a few problems and ask the candidate to review it. It reveals how they read code, what they prioritise and how they communicate feedback.
2. **Design discussion.** A system problem close to your own, with time to ask questions. Score how they gather requirements, name trade-offs and handle failure.
3. **Pairing on a small task.** Useful where collaboration is central. Be explicit about the tools allowed, including AI assistants, and say what you want to learn.
4. **Behavioural conversation.** Ask for specific examples: a production incident, a disagreement, a decision that turned out wrong.

Avoid algorithm puzzles unless the work involves them. Use a written rubric and have interviewers score independently before comparing notes, which cuts the effect of the loudest voice. Decide your policy on AI assistance in assessments and tell candidates.

## Which skills are shifting?

**Working with AI coding tools.** Assistants now draft functions, tests and documentation. Engineers who use them well still read the output critically, write clear specifications and understand the system well enough to spot subtle errors. Hire for judgment about what to accept and what to rewrite.

**Systems thinking.** As routine implementation becomes faster, the premium shifts toward designing, integrating and operating systems that behave well under load and failure.

**Operational ownership.** Engineers who run what they build, with monitoring, alerting and incident review, are valuable. Ask about a system they improved after an incident.

**Security and privacy awareness.** Basic secure-development practice is expected of all engineers, not only specialists.

**Communication.** Writing design documents and giving clear code review feedback matter more as teams distribute across locations.

## How do you think about compensation and location?

Pay varies with level, specialism, company stage and location, and published salary pages often disagree. Decide your approach to location, whether one band, geographic tiers or a mix, and apply it consistently. Inconsistent exceptions are a quiet cause of resentment. Build ranges from your own bands, public wage data and the reasons your candidates decline. If equity is part of the offer, explain the type, vesting and what happens if the company is sold, without implying a value.

## Why do engineers leave?

- **Unclear impact.** People leave when they cannot see how their work matters. Connect projects to outcomes.
- **Heavy on-call without support.** Noisy alerts and thin rotas burn people out. Fix the sources of noise.
- **Poor tooling and slow builds.** Waiting for long builds each day wears people down. Investing in developer experience is a retention measure.
- **Stalled growth.** Offer a senior individual contributor path with scope, not only management.
- **Reorganisations without explanation.** Frequent changes in priorities without reasons erode trust.
- **Unfair promotion.** Publish the criteria and calibrate across teams.

## An illustrative example: the cost of a long build

Assume an engineering team of twenty, where each engineer waits for a build or test run eight times a day and each wait costs three minutes of lost focus. That is twenty-four minutes a day per person, about eight hours of focus a day across the team. Whether the true figure is higher or lower, the exercise shows that tooling improvements can be compared with the cost of replacing a frustrated engineer. These numbers are placeholders chosen for the arithmetic.

## How should onboarding work?

Prepare a working environment before day one. Give a small, real first task, and aim for a merged change in the first week or two. Name a buddy and a manager who will meet weekly. Document the architecture and the reasons behind it. Ask each new hire at thirty days to update the onboarding documentation with what they found confusing; the best onboarding guide is written by the last person who needed it.

## How can you keep the interview process fair and fast?

A long loop loses good candidates and rarely improves decisions. Aim for a first screen, one practical exercise, one design or collaboration conversation and one conversation about working style, with each interviewer assigned a distinct purpose so that candidates are not asked the same questions four times. Tell candidates the full process at the start, including how long each stage takes and when to expect an answer. Keep a record of why candidates were rejected, in a short fixed list, and check periodically whether the reasons relate to the job. If you find that a particular school, previous employer or background is over-represented among those you advance, examine the reason and adjust your criteria. Measure the days between stages, because most delays sit in scheduling and feedback, not in the interviews themselves.

Whatever you change, change one thing at a time and watch the stage data for a quarter before changing the next, so you can tell which change helped.
